content: Pre-eclampsia is a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy that remains a leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide, with the majority of deaths occurring in developing countries. It is a multi-organ syndrome that typically arises after 20 weeks of gestation and is characterized by new-onset hypertension accompanied by maternal end-organ dysfunction and/or fetal growth restriction. Despite its significant impact on maternal and fetal health, there is currently no effective treatment for pre-eclampsia. The severity of pre-eclampsia is not universally defined, but the International Society for the Study of Hypertension in Pregnancy (ISSHP) has identified key factors that indicate severe disease. These include difficulty in controlling blood pressure, clinical deterioration (such as the development of HELLP syndrome, which involves hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets), impending eclampsia, worsening thrombocytopenia, or worsening fetal growth restriction. Symptoms of HELLP syndrome may include upper right abdominal pain, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and increased swelling. Pre-eclampsia poses significant risks to the fetus, contributing to 12% of cases of fetal growth restriction and up to 19% of preterm births. The exact cause of pre-eclampsia is unknown, but it is believed to result from a complex interplay between the mother, fetus, and placenta. A key process in pregnancy is placentation, during which the blastocyst (early embryo) attaches to the uterine lining and remodels the maternal spiral arteries to ensure adequate blood flow to the placenta. If this process is disrupted, placental development may be impaired, leading to reduced blood flow and uteroplacental hypoxia, as seen in pre-eclampsia. One hypothesis suggests that placental hypoperfusion in pre-eclampsia induces oxidative stress, characterized by the overproduction of reactive oxygen species and depletion of antioxidants. This oxidative stress, combined with an exaggerated inflammatory response, may lead to endothelial cell activation and damage. Endothelial dysfunction is a hallmark of pre-eclampsia and manifests clinically as hypertension and proteinuria. A woman’s susceptibility to oxidative stress may depend on factors such as lipid profile, hyperhomocysteinemia, genetic predisposition, and dietary antioxidant intake. Screening for pre-eclampsia is a critical component of antenatal care. Current screening methods include blood pressure measurement and urinalysis for proteinuria. However, these methods have limitations, as 15% to 25% of women with gestational hypertension progress to pre-eclampsia. Doppler ultrasound to assess uterine artery resistance is a promising non-invasive test, but no screening test has yet demonstrated high predictive value. Preventive strategies for pre-eclampsia focus on antenatal surveillance, lifestyle modifications, nutritional supplementation, and pharmacological interventions. Aspirin, an antiplatelet agent, has been shown to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia by 17% in high-risk women. Calcium supplementation (≥1 g/day) significantly reduces the risk, particularly in women with low dietary calcium intake. Antithrombotic therapies, such as low molecular weight heparin, may also decrease the risk in women with placental dysfunction. Melatonin, a potent antioxidant, has been proposed as a potential preventive and therapeutic agent for pre-eclampsia. Melatonin is a lipid-soluble hormone produced by the pineal gland and is known for its role in regulating circadian rhythms. It also acts as a direct scavenger of reactive oxygen species and upregulates antioxidant enzymes such as glutathione peroxidase, superoxide dismutase, and catalase. Melatonin has been shown to reduce oxidative stress and improve clinical outcomes in various conditions, including neonatal asphyxia and sepsis. In the context of human reproduction, melatonin is present in follicular fluid and plays a role in oocyte maturation and quality, potentially improving pregnancy outcomes in assisted reproductive technology. Studies have shown no increase in abnormalities in babies born from melatonin-treated pregnancies. Although there is limited data on the prolonged use of melatonin in later stages of pregnancy, preliminary findings from the PAMPR trial suggest no harm to mothers or babies. Melatonin has several characteristics that make it an attractive candidate for use in pregnancy. It crosses the placenta and blood-brain barrier and has an excellent safety profile with no known adverse effects. Reduced melatonin levels have been observed in women with pre-eclampsia, and placental tissues express melatonin receptors, suggesting a potential protective role against oxidative stress. Animal studies have demonstrated that melatonin administration reduces fetal hypoxia, improves neurodevelopment, and decreases oxidative stress and brain injury in models of fetal growth restriction and asphyxia. In rat models, melatonin has been shown to protect placental mitochondria from oxidative damage, improve placental function, and increase birth weight. These findings suggest that melatonin may mitigate the effects of oxidative stress and inflammation associated with pre-eclampsia. Importantly, animal and human studies to date have not identified any harm associated with melatonin treatment. Given the role of oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of pre-eclampsia, melatonin’s antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties make it a promising candidate for preventing the condition and its complications. Further research is needed to evaluate its efficacy and safety in preventing pre-eclampsia in human pregnancies.
